prompt: H2 holds `=E2*F2`. You copy H2 and paste it into H40. What formula is in H40?
hint: Every address moves by the distance the formula moved.

choices.text: `=E2*F2`, the formula exactly as it was typed
choices.why: That is what an absolute reference would give. These addresses are relative, so they moved 38 rows with the formula.
The formula moved from row 2 to row 40, 38 rows, so row 2 becomes row 40, not 41.
Right. The bags and the price of row 40, read from row 40.

choices.text: `=$E$40*$F$40`, with dollars added by the paste
choices.why: A paste never adds dollar signs. It moves relative addresses and leaves the rest as written.

prompt: With the `Revenue` column filled from H2 to H109, what does `=SUM(H2:H109)` return?
hint: Type it in an empty cell outside the data.

prompt: You double-click the fill handle of H2 and the formulas stop at row 60 instead of row 109. What is the likely cause?
hint: How does the double-click decide where to stop?

choices.text: The neighbouring column has an empty cell in row 61
choices.why: Right. The double-click fills as far as the column beside it has data, and a gap stops it without a word.

choices.text: One double-click copies a formula at most 60 times
choices.why: There is no such limit; it fills to row 109 when the neighbouring column is complete.

choices.text: The formula has no dollar signs, so it cannot travel further
choices.why: Dollar signs decide which addresses move, not how far a formula can be copied.

choices.text: Rows 61 to 109 are formatted as text
choices.why: A format changes how a value is drawn. It does not stop the fill.

prompt: H2 holds `=E2*F2`. Copied one column to the right, into I2, it shows `#VALUE!`. Why?
hint: Read the formula that arrived in I2.

choices.text: A formula cannot be pasted into a column with no header
choices.why: A header is for the reader. Excel pastes formulas anywhere.

choices.text: I2 became `=F2*G2`, and G2 is the text `Wholesale`
choices.why: Right. Both addresses moved one column, and a price times a word is an error.

choices.text: Excel never multiplies two cells from different columns
choices.why: H2 itself multiplies two different columns, E and F.

choices.text: The paste kept `=E2*F2` but the result is too large for I
choices.why: The formula changed, and nothing about the size of a number gives `#VALUE!`.

prompt: J2 holds `=H2/L2`, with the total in L2. Filled down, J3 shows `#DIV/0!`. Why?
hint: Click J3 and read its formula.

choices.text: H3 is zero, so the sale has no revenue
choices.why: H3 is 1972. The zero is in the other half of the division.

choices.text: The total in L2 is too large to divide by
choices.why: Any number other than zero can be divided by. The problem is which cell J3 divides by.

choices.text: J3 holds `=H3/L3`, and L3 is empty
choices.why: Right. The reference to the total moved down a row, and an empty cell counts as zero.

choices.text: Filling down always breaks a formula that divides
choices.why: Filling down `=H2/$L$2` divides correctly on every row.

prompt: Match each way of writing the address to what happens to it when the formula is copied down and across.
hint: A dollar fixes whatever comes right after it.

pairs.right: Stays on row 2, the column moves
Stays in column L, the row moves

right_distractors: Jumps to the last row of the data

prompt: A colleague's share column uses `=H2/SUM(H2:H109)` filled down. No cell shows an error. What is wrong?
hint: Write out the formula that lands in J3.

choices.text: Nothing: the SUM inside the formula keeps the total fixed
choices.why: Only dollar signs keep an address fixed. Inside SUM, both ends of H2:H109 move with the row.

choices.text: Each row divides by a total that starts at its own row, so the column adds to far more than 100%
choices.why: Right. J3 divides by H3:H110 and J109 by itself; the column adds to 579%.

choices.text: The shares are right but they will not survive a sort
choices.why: They are wrong before any sort: from J3 down, every denominator leaves out the rows above.

choices.text: SUM cannot be used inside a division
choices.why: It can; the trouble is only that its range is relative.

prompt: The cursor is inside `L2` in the formula bar, and you press F4 four times. Put the forms in the order they appear.
hint: The first press fixes both halves; the last frees them.
trap: The two forms with one dollar are easy to swap: the row is fixed before the column.

prompt: In the discount grid on `Products`, what does J5 show: `CER1K` at 10% off, rounded to whole reais?
hint: R$ 118 less 10%, then ROUND to 0 decimals.

prompt: In `=ROUND($F2*(1-I$1),0)`, what does the dollar in `I$1` do?
hint: Ask in which direction this address must not move.

choices.text: It keeps the discount on row 1 when the formula is copied down
choices.why: Right. Copied across, it still moves to J and K, so each column reads its own discount.

choices.text: It keeps the discount in column I when the formula is copied across
choices.why: That would be `$I1`. With `I$1`, the column moves, which is why the 10% column reads J1.

choices.text: It rounds the discount to a whole percentage
choices.why: Rounding is ROUND's job, on the result. A dollar sign only decides what moves.

choices.text: It marks the discount as a currency amount in reais
choices.why: The dollar in an address has nothing to do with money.

prompt: A grid has months in A2:A13 and channels in B1:D1, and the formula in B2 needs one of each. Which pair of references fills all 36 cells correctly from B2?
hint: The month must not leave column A; the channel must not leave row 1.

choices.text: `A$2` for the month and `$B1` for the channel
choices.why: Reversed. `A$2` stays on row 2, so every row would read January, and `$B1` stays in column B.

choices.text: `$A$2` and `$B$1`, so nothing can drift
choices.why: Then all 36 cells read January and the first channel: one value repeated.

choices.text: `$A2` for the month and `B$1` for the channel
choices.why: Right. The month keeps its column and follows the row; the channel keeps its row and follows the column.

choices.text: `A2` and `B1`, since each cell is on its own row and column
choices.why: Copied across, `A2` becomes B2, a cell of the grid, and copied down, `B1` becomes B2 too.

prompt: Typed with no dollars in I2, `=ROUND(F2*(1-I1),0)` is copied to I3, which shows -5016. What did I3 compute?
hint: Write out the formula in I3.

choices.text: The list price of `SUL1K` times one minus 39, the price just computed in I2
choices.why: Right. `I1` moved to `I2`, which holds a price, not a discount.

choices.text: The list price of `SUL250` with a discount of 5%
choices.why: That is what I2 computes. In I3 both addresses have moved one row.

choices.text: A circular reference, which Excel shows as a negative number
choices.why: Nothing refers to itself here, and a circular reference does not produce -5016.

choices.text: The unit cost in G3 instead of the list price
choices.why: Copying down moves the row, not the column; `F2` became `F3`, still the list price.

prompt: Which of these does Excel refuse as a defined name? Choose all that apply.
hint: Spaces, and anything that already means a cell.

choices.why: Q1 is a cell address, so it cannot also be a name.

choices.text: `Total Revenue`
choices.why: A name has no spaces. `TotalRevenue` or `Total_Revenue` works.
Column TAX exists, so TAX2025 is a cell.

choices.text: `Total_Revenue`
choices.why: An underscore is allowed, and it is the usual way to separate words in a name.

choices.text: `_rate`
choices.why: A name may start with an underscore.

prompt: The name `Revenue` refers to `=Sales!$H$2:$H$109`. A 109th sale is added in row 110. What does `=SUM(Revenue)` do?
hint: Is a name a range or a column?

choices.text: It includes the new sale, because a name follows its column
choices.why: A name is a fixed range. Rows added below it are outside it.

choices.text: It shows `#REF!` until the name is edited
choices.why: Nothing it refers to was deleted, so there is no error.

choices.text: It counts the new sale twice, once in the name and once in H110
choices.why: H110 is not in the name at all.

choices.text: It leaves the new sale out, and nothing shows an error
choices.why: Right. The name means H2:H109 and nothing else. Lesson 7's tables grow with the data.

prompt: `=H2/$L$2` and `=H2/TotalRevenue` give the same numbers. What does the second one add?
hint: Think of the person who opens the file next month.

choices.text: A faster calculation
choices.why: Both point at the same cell; neither is faster.

choices.text: It says what it divides by
choices.why: Right. The name carries the meaning that the address hides.

choices.text: A total that grows with the data
choices.why: TotalRevenue points at L2. What grows is lesson 7's tables.

choices.text: Protection against the cell being deleted
choices.why: Delete L2's column and the name refers to `#REF!` too.

prompt: A defined name is known everywhere in the workbook unless you choose a sheet as its ___ when you create it.
hint: The Name Manager shows it in a column of its own.

prompt: J2:J109 hold `=H2/$L$2` and its copies. Column L is deleted. What does column J show?
hint: The cell the formulas named no longer exists.

choices.text: `#DIV/0!`, because the total is now zero
choices.why: The total was not set to zero; the cell itself is gone, and Excel says so differently.

choices.text: `#REF!` in every cell
choices.why: Right. The formula now reads `=H2/#REF!`. Ctrl+Z brings it back if you act at once.

choices.text: The old shares, kept from before the delete
choices.why: Formulas recalculate. There is nothing to keep once their reference is gone.

choices.text: 0, because an empty cell counts as zero
choices.why: An empty cell would give `#DIV/0!`. Here the cell does not exist at all.

prompt: L2 holds `=SUM(H2:H109)`. Row 50, sale S1049, is deleted. What does L2 show now?
hint: The range shrinks to fit; H50 was 9 bags at R$ 116.

prompt: Somebody typed `1044` over the formula in H50. Later E50 is corrected from 9 bags to 10. What happens?
hint: Which cells still contain formulas?

choices.text: H50 becomes 1160 and the total becomes 51,610
choices.why: That is what the formula would do. H50 holds a number now, and a number does not recalculate.

choices.text: H50 turns red, because Excel marks a typed number among formulas
choices.why: No such mark appears; that is why this failure needs Go To Special or Show Formulas to find.

choices.text: H50 stays 1044, the total stays 51,494, and no cell shows an error
choices.why: Right. The total is R$ 116 short, and nothing on the screen says so.

choices.text: E50 refuses the new value while H50 depends on it
choices.why: Any cell can be changed; H50 no longer depends on E50 at all.

prompt: Which command selects every typed value in H2:H109, so a number pasted over a formula is found?
hint: It selects by what a cell holds, not by what it shows.

choices.text: Formulas › Error Checking › Circular References
choices.why: That lists cells whose formula depends on itself. A typed number is not a formula at all.

choices.text: Formulas › Name Manager
choices.why: That lists names, not the contents of a column.

choices.text: Home › Find & Select › Go To Special, then Constants
choices.why: Right. In a healthy Revenue column it finds nothing.

choices.text: Home › Find & Select › Replace, with nothing in Find what
choices.why: Replace changes text in cells; it selects nothing, and an empty search finds nothing to change.

prompt: `=ROUND($F2*(1-I$1),0)` in `Products!I2` is copied to K4. What formula is in K4?
hint: Two rows down and two columns across; move only what has no dollar in front of it.

choices.why: The row of `$F2` has no dollar, so it moves with the formula, to `$F4`.
Right. The price follows the row in column F; the discount follows the column on row 1.
`$F` cannot move across, and `$1` cannot move down: both halves moved the wrong way here.
`I$1` has no dollar before the column, so copied two columns across it becomes `K$1`.

prompt: A total, `=SUM(H:H)`, is typed in H111. What happens?
hint: Which cells does H:H contain?

choices.text: It adds the 108 sales and shows 51,494
choices.why: H:H includes H111, so the total would have to contain itself.

choices.text: It shows `#REF!`, because H111 is outside the data
choices.why: Nothing was deleted. The problem is a cell that depends on its own value.

choices.text: A circular reference: Excel warns, and it shows 0
choices.why: Right. Totals belong outside the column they add, as L2 was.

choices.text: Excel moves the total to the first empty column
choices.why: Excel never moves a formula on its own.

prompt: The largest share in the share column belongs to the sale with the largest revenue. What is that sale's revenue, in reais?
hint: `=MAX(H2:H109)`, or find the row where `=MAX(J2:J109)` sits.

prompt: Why does the lesson put the total that the shares divide by in L2, beside the data, and not in H110 under it?
hint: What would a sum of column H include?

choices.text: A cell in column L calculates faster than one in column H
choices.why: Position does not change the speed of a formula.

choices.text: Excel does not allow a formula below the last row of data in a column
choices.why: It allows it. The trouble is what other formulas then count.

choices.text: So that it can be given a defined name
choices.why: A cell in column H can be named too.

choices.text: A total inside the data gets counted by every sum over the column
choices.why: Right. `=SUM(H:H)` would add it, and a total that includes itself is a circular reference.
